To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CD4 regulatory T cell development and function are enhanced in the lung of mice chronically exposed to Ag, and that CD4 regulatory cells are able to suppress type 2 immune response but not bronchial hyperresponsiveness.

CD4 T cells that are specific for an Ag that is deposited in the lung are rendered tolerant by this Ag, and this tolerance is reversed in the presence of the OVA-specific DO 11.10 T cell receptor transgene.
CD25+ CD26 regulatory T cells are induced in the airways of mice with Ag-specific airway inflammation, and that these cells suppress type 2 immune reactions in the airways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CD25+ CD 4 regulatory T cells in the development of airway disease.
the mechanisms of airway disease in asthma.
the mechanisms that underlie the development of chronic allergic inflammation of the airways and the mechanisms that regulate the development of allergic airway disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CD25+ regulatory T cells can suppress the development of allergic airway disease but are not able to prevent the development of bronchoconstriction.
CD25+ CD2 regulatory T cells are not sufficient for the prevention of bronchial asthma.
CD25+ CD25 regulatory T cells suppress type 2 immune response in the airway but do not affect bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CD25+ CD2 regulatory T cells are not sufficient to suppress the development of bronchopulmonary hyperreactivity.
CD25+ CD2 regulatory T cells suppress type 2 immune response, but not airway hyperreactivity, induced by chronic Ag exposure in the lungs.

chronic airway Ag deposition leads to the generation of CD25+ CD25+ T cells that can suppress allergic type 1 and type 2 immune reactions but have no effect on airway reactivity to contractile stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD25+ CD2 T cells are present in the lungs of mice with chronic airway disease and are capable of suppressing type 2 immunity, but are ineffective in suppressing airway hyperreactivity.
CD25+ CD3 T cells can be induced to develop in the lung of mice with airway allergic disease and that they function to regulate type 2 immune response.
CD4+ CD25+ Tregs can be generated in vivo in response to Ag exposure and can suppress type 2 immune reactions.
